1. Core Clinical Tension: A 60-year-old female lung transplant recipient with no personal travel or exposure history developed painful occipital subcutaneous nodules, flexor tenosynovitis, and multifocal hepatic abscesses refractory to broad-spectrum antibacterials. The clinical tension lies in recognizing disseminated donor-derived tuberculosis presenting primarily with extrapulmonary manifestations (tenosynovitis, cutaneous nodules, and liver abscesses) rather than pulmonary cavitation.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs immediately following admission triage, physical examination, baseline laboratory tests (marked leukopenia/lymphopenia), and initial cross-sectional imaging (chest CT and abdominal MRI showing multiple hepatic lesions, and hand MRI demonstrating flexor tenosynovitis), before invasive biopsy, aspiration, and microbiologic staining.
3. Differential Distinctions: Common pyogenic bacterial flexor tenosynovitis and cellulitis were excluded by lack of response to linezolid and ceftriaxone. Invasive fungal infections and disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) were strong initial possibilities given cutaneous-articular involvement under heavy immunosuppression, but mass spectrometry and rapid culture of biopsied tissue confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex.
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old woman with a history of bilateral lung transplantation for severe emphysema presented with painful occipital subcutaneous nodules and painful swelling of her right index finger approximately 74 days post-transplantation. Induction immunosuppression had consisted of basiliximab, with maintenance therapy comprising prednisone, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil. Her post-transplant course had been complicated by right lung graft lobar torsion requiring right pneumonectomy on postoperative day 2, treatment for acute rejection with pulsed methylprednisolone and rituximab at post-transplant day 30, and parainfluenza infection managed with steroids and intravenous immunoglobulin at post-transplant day 54.

Two weeks prior to admission, she was evaluated in an outpatient clinic for tender occipital nodules and index finger swelling and was prescribed a 14-day course of linezolid and ceftriaxone for presumptive cellulitis. Despite completing antibiotics, the finger and scalp pain worsened, and she developed nausea, vomiting, chills, and diaphoresis, prompting hospital admission. Epidemiologic history was notable for lifelong residence in Kansas without any international travel or residence outside the United States. She owned domestic dogs and cats but denied bites or scratches, livestock contact, freshwater exposure, gardening, trauma, unpasteurized dairy consumption, or prior history of incarceration or homelessness.

On physical examination, she was afebrile and well-appearing. Examination of the scalp revealed two exquisitely tender, firm, non-mobile nodules in the occipital region without erythema, fluctuance, or drainage. Her right index finger was markedly erythematous and edematous with limited active and passive range of motion. Pulmonary examination revealed absent breath sounds over the right hemithorax and clear breath sounds over the left lung. Abdominal examination was soft and non-tender without hepatosplenomegaly, and there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy or rash.

Laboratory studies demonstrated leukopenia with a white-cell count of 3,000 per cubic millimeter and absolute lymphopenia of 600 per cubic millimeter. Non-contrast chest CT and abdominal MRI revealed numerous new rim-enhancing, hypoattenuating hepatic lesions concerning for multifocal abscesses. Right hand MRI demonstrated a peripherally enhancing 1.3-cm fluid collection along the palmar aspect of the index finger associated with the flexor tendon sheath.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pyogenic bacterial cellulitis and acute flexor tenosynovitis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Initially suspected and treated outpatient; ruled out by failure of a 14-day course of linezolid and ceftriaxone, progression to systemic symptoms, and emergence of multifocal hepatic abscesses.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Two weeks later, she presented to clinic and was started on linezolid and ceftriaxone for cellulitis. Shortly after completing a 2-week course of antibiotics, pain worsened and she developed nausea, vomiting, chills, and diaphoresis prompting hospital admission.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Strongly considered when acid-fast bacilli were identified on synovial fluid and liver histology in an immunosuppressed host with skin and soft tissue involvement; excluded when MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry identified the organism as Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex rather than an atypical mycobacterial species.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Direct staining of finger tissue was positive with 1-9 acid fast bacilli (AFB)/10 high-power field and empiric treatment for disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) with linezolid, cefoxitin, azithromycin, and moxifloxacin was promptly initiated.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Invasive fungal infection (e.g., endemic mycosis, Aspergillus, Candida)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A high-probability consideration in a lung transplant recipient receiving augmented immunosuppression with glucocorticoids and rituximab; ruled out by negative fungal stains (GMS) and absence of fungal growth.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and Grocott Methenamine Silver (GMS) stains were negative for organisms... Transthoracic echocardiogram and brain MRI were unremarkable. Extensive infectious work-up remained negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Histopathologic evaluation of core needle liver biopsy and surgical drainage of the flexor tendon sheath demonstrating necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with acid-fast bacilli, coupled with culture identification via MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry as Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, established donor-transmitted disseminated tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Both liver and tendon histopathology noted granulomatous inflammation with AFB... Finger and liver tissue cultures grew AFB after 4 days identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry as Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex.

editor_comments: Admission narrative strictly truncated prior to invasive tissue sampling (liver biopsy and tenosynovial I&D). Preserves all immunosuppression history, failed outpatient antibiotic courses, and baseline imaging. Zero mention of Mycobacterium or donor origin in the case presentation.
